title: Writing the history
hook: Sikh and other historians have written the Sikh story in many languages
tomorrow: Three hundred years of the Khalsa

segments.voice: Yesterday, fiber optics, and your line was light in glass. Today, a different kind of careful work: keeping the story itself.

Who keeps a people's story? Start smaller, with a shoebox on a high shelf. Inside: letters in a grandfather's handwriting, a photo with names penciled on the back, a ration card, a train ticket. Nobody has opened it in years. When the last person who can read that handwriting is gone, the box becomes a puzzle. Some families have a box like that. A whole people has one too, and someone has to open it, read it, and write down what it says. Today: who wrote the history.
screen: `A SHOEBOX ON A HIGH SHELF.` → `HANDWRITING NOBODY CAN READ.` → `WHO WROTE THE HISTORY?`

segments.voice: First, the earliest tellers. Bhai Gurdas, whom this path met long ago, wrote verses about the Gurus and the early Sikhs. Alongside them came the janamsakhis, collections of stories about Guru Nanak's life. Different janamsakhis tell some of the same stories in different ways, and historians read them with care, as treasured stories rather than as a diary. Second, insiders and outsiders. Max Arthur Macauliffe, an officer in British India, wrote a large English work, The Sikh Religion, and worked closely with Sikh scholars, among them Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha, who also compiled his own Punjabi encyclopedia, the Mahan Kosh. The story was written down in Punjabi, Persian, English and Urdu, by Sikhs and by others, and each writer saw it from where they stood. Third, the arguments. Historians don't always agree. They weigh one account against another, and ask who wrote it, when, and why. Not long ago this path asked you to read both sides of a hard question; good history keeps doing that. Fourth, the root. At Ang 951 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Amar Das says that the stories of the elders make children into worthy children. The stories matter because they shape who comes next. But a story only reaches the next generation if someone keeps it, by telling it, or by writing it down.
screen: `BHAI GURDAS AND THE JANAMSAKHIS.` · `INSIDERS AND OUTSIDERS TOGETHER.` · `WHO WROTE IT, WHEN, AND WHY?` · `THE STORIES OF THE ELDERS.` · then, large: `WRITE IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one family story nobody has written down: how two people met, how someone crossed a border, what a grandparent did when the money ran out. See one face, one place, one moment, and find the first sentence you'd use to write it, saying it silently once, then again. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and give thanks for the people in the story.
Bhai Gurdas. One of the earliest tellers of the Sikh story, whose verses about the Gurus stand alongside the janamsakhis, Macauliffe and Bhai Kahn Singh. Today's word.
Your line: write it down. Even an old shoebox can speak again. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1021 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE HUNDRED YEARS OF THE KHALSA.`

howItsDone: Sikh history is kept in Bhai Gurdas's verses, the janamsakhis, later Punjabi and Persian chronicles, and modern histories in many languages; families and gurdwaras also pass the stories on by telling them, especially at gurpurabs and in katha.

chat.says: If the janamsakhis tell some stories differently, how do historians use them at all?
options: They read them with care, as treasured stories, and ask who wrote each account, when, and why.
They throw out any story that two janamsakhis don't tell in exactly the same way.
They pick the oldest one and treat it as a word-for-word diary of Guru Nanak's life.
chat.meaning: Historians read the janamsakhis as treasured stories rather than a diary, weighing each account by who wrote it, when and why.
